title: [B2 • Band 6.0] Bài 320: The Vertical Frontier: Elevators & Cities
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 320 (LEVEL B2 • BAND 6.0)

The Vertical Frontier: Elevators, Steel, and Urban Stratification

Paragraph 1. Until the mid-nineteenth century, the vertical expansion of world cities was held back by a universal biological constraint: the human knee. Although builders had long possessed the technical ability to erect stone towers beyond ten storeys, urban buildings rarely climbed higher than five or six floors. Climbing past the fifth flight of stairs was physically exhausting, turning top-floor garrets into cheap, undesirable rooms rented by domestic servants, poor students, and struggling artists. Wealthy families occupied the prestigious first and second floors—the piano nobile—enjoying easy street access without the strain of climbing. Pre-industrial cities were therefore divided horizontally by wealth, yet shared vertically under the same roof.

Paragraph 2. This ancient spatial order was overturned in May 1854 at the New York Crystal Palace exhibition. Standing on an open hoisting platform suspended high above a nervous crowd, inventor Elisha Graves Otis ordered the main cable severed. Instead of plunging downward, the platform fell mere inches before his spring-operated safety brake locked onto toothed guide rails. Combined with the Bessemer steel-making process, which replaced thick load-bearing stone walls with lightweight steel skeletons, Otis's safety elevator removed the vertical ceiling on urban growth.

Paragraph 3. In Up: The Vertical City, urban sociologist Dr. Ronald Kroll examines how the elevator reversed social geography almost overnight. Upper floors, once avoided for stair fatigue, swiftly became the most coveted real estate in the city. High above street dust, foul smells, and traffic roar, the humble attic was reborn as the luxury penthouse, offering abundant sunlight, clean air, and sweeping views. Meanwhile, ground and lower levels were demoted to retail shops and secondary offices.

Paragraph 4. Kroll argues that the elevator functioned as far more than a mechanical convenience; it became a powerful engine of social separation. In low-rise cities, citizens from contrasting economic backgrounds constantly crossed paths on stairwells and sidewalks. In modern skyscrapers, however, high-speed elevators operate as enclosed private transit cabins, carrying corporate elites directly from underground garages to cloud-level suites while completely bypassing public civic spaces. By dissolving the physical friction of height, Otis's invention did not merely lift bodies skyward—it insulated the affluent from everyday democratic city life.

groups.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A–F, below.
endings: A. municipal leaders immediately banned all low-rise apartments.
B. tall buildings no longer required massive stone walls for support.
C. elevators proved too expensive to install inside commercial towers.
D. they wanted easy street access without the ordeal of climbing stairs.
E. wealthy residents can travel privately without entering public spaces.
F. hoisting platforms could stop safely even if their main cables snapped.

q9.text: What was a key social feature of pre-industrial apartment buildings?
options: A. Poor citizens enjoyed cleaner air than lower-floor landlords.
B. People of different economic classes lived inside the same building.
C. Wealthy owners lived in rural villages outside city walls.
D. Employers were legally forced to rent ground floors to servants.

options: A. It ran silently on electric batteries rather than steam.
B. It was built entirely from lightweight timber frames.
C. It was designed specifically for underground coal mines.
D. It featured an automatic brake that prevented deadly falls.

options: A. They turned upper levels into storage rooms for machinery.

q12.text: What is Dr. Kroll's central criticism of the modern skyscraper elevator?
options: A. It deepens social isolation by cutting off the wealthy from public life.
B. It wastes unsustainable amounts of municipal electricity.
C. It breaks down frequently during severe urban windstorms.
D. It prevents architects from installing natural ventilation shafts.
